Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: Which chemotherapy class is named as a risk factor for acute myeloid leukemia?
opts: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark treatment of chronic-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia and are added to chemotherapy for Philadelphia-positive lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: they are therapy here, not a listed cause.

Hypomethylating agents are low-intensity treatment for unfit patients with acute myeloid leukemia and for higher-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: they treat myeloid cancers; alkylators are the listed risk.
Janus kinase inhibitors are palliative targeted treatment for myelofibrosis. Tell: the chemotherapy named as a cause of acute myeloid leukemia is the alkylator class.

Correct. Chemical risk factors for acute myeloid leukemia include benzene, petroleum and certain chemotherapies, specifically alkylators. Leukemia arising after treatment of another cancer is therapy-related, a form of secondary disease with poor outcomes.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: Which complication is listed for myelofibrosis?
opts: Acquired von Willebrand factor shortage explains bleeding with high platelets in essential thrombocythemia. Tell: myelofibrosis can progress to secondary acute myeloid leukemia.
Itching with warm baths or showers is the classic symptom of polycythemia vera, not a complication of myelofibrosis. Tell: myelofibrosis complications include leukemic progression.
Correct. Complications of myelofibrosis include severe splenomegaly, portal hypertension, bleeding and progression to secondary acute myeloid leukemia, which carries poor outcomes.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the emergent presentation of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: myelofibrosis complications are splenic, portal and leukemic.

set1.topic: Polycythemia vera
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: Which mutation commonly causes polycythemia vera?
opts: Correct. Polycythemia vera commonly occurs as a result of a JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) mutation. Myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia also arise from mutations in the same Janus kinase pathway.

The BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) fusion from the chromosome 9 and 22 translocation is the hallmark of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: a red cell overproduction disorder points to the Janus kinase 2 mutation.
The PML-RARA (promyelocytic leukemia-retinoic acid receptor alpha) fusion from chromosomes 15 and 17 causes acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: polycythemia vera is a Janus kinase 2 disease.
Hyperdiploidy, excess chromosome copies, is the favorable childhood finding in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: the myeloproliferative neoplasms share Janus kinase pathway mutations.

set1.q: Which lab pattern fits chronic-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia?
opts: An elevated red cell mass is polycythemia vera; in chronic myelogenous leukemia the hematocrit is not elevated. Tell: the chronic myelogenous leukemia excess is white cells and platelets.
Correct. Labs show marked leukocytosis, often above 100,000 and up to 500,000, thrombocytosis and anemia, with usually very low blasts unless the disease is in accelerated or blast phase.
Low counts with abnormal-looking neutrophils describe myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia raises the white count and platelets.
Blasts at or above 20% define acute leukemia; chronic-phase disease has fewer than 5%. Tell: chronic phase has very few blasts.

set1.q: About what share of all lymphomas are non-Hodgkin lymphomas?
opts: About 10% is the share of Hodgkin lymphoma, the type characterized by few Reed-Sternberg cells. Tell: the two shares add to 100, and non-Hodgkin is the large majority.
An even split understates non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which makes up about 90% of lymphomas. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma is the small group at about 10%.
Seventy percent understates it; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is about 90% of lymphomas, leaving about 10% for Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: the split is nine to one.
Correct. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma accounts for about 90% of all lymphomas and includes both B-cell and T-cell lymphomas. Hodgkin lymphoma, with its Reed-Sternberg cells, makes up the remaining 10%.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 15

set1.topic: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: management and prognosis
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: In acute lymphoblastic leukemia, when is allogeneic stem cell transplant used?
opts: Hyperdiploidy in children carries a favorable prognosis, and five-year survival under 15 is about 90% with intensive chemotherapy. Tell: transplant is kept for adverse-risk or relapsed disease.
Induction is the first phase of the intensive chemotherapy regimen; transplant does not replace it. Tell: transplant follows for adverse-risk or relapsed disease, where feasible.
Adults start with induction, consolidation and maintenance chemotherapy; transplant is reserved for adverse-risk or relapsed disease. Tell: the trigger is risk or relapse, not adult age by itself.

Correct. Allogeneic stem cell transplant is used where feasible for adverse-risk acute lymphoblastic leukemia or relapsed disease. Most patients start with intensive chemotherapy, with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor added if Philadelphia-positive.

set1.q: Which group with acute myeloid leukemia has the lowest five-year survival?
opts: Younger patients are listed with favorable risk among the best outcomes. Tell: survival falls with age and is lowest over 70.
Patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia who survive the initial presentation have an excellent prognosis, above 90% cure. Tell: the lowest five-year survival is in patients over 70.

Correct. Survival is lowest for patients over 70, only 5% at five years, and for adverse-risk or secondary disease, about 10% overall. It is highest, apart from acute promyelocytic leukemia, for favorable-risk disease and younger patients.
Favorable-risk acute myeloid leukemia has the highest survival outside the promyelocytic subtype, about two thirds alive at five years. Tell: the worst outlook is age over 70.

set1.topic: Essential thrombocythemia
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: Which clotting complications are named for essential thrombocythemia?
opts: Disseminated intravascular coagulation belongs to acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: essential thrombocythemia is about clots from too many platelets.
Progression to leukemia is the concern in myelofibrosis and, rarely, polycythemia vera. Tell: the essential thrombocythemia list is clotting.

Correct. Complications of essential thrombocythemia are clotting, including stroke (cerebrovascular accident) and heart attack (myocardial infarction). Presentation may also be headaches, fatigue, paresthesias or vision changes from clotting.
Portal hypertension is a complication of myelofibrosis with severe splenomegaly. Tell: essential thrombocythemia clots in arteries of the brain and heart.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 54

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: Which cell characterizes Hodgkin lymphoma?
opts: Arrested promyelocytes define acute promyelocytic leukemia, a myeloid cancer caused by the chromosome 15 and 17 translocation. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma is lymphoid tissue with Reed-Sternberg cells.

Lymphoblasts are the very immature cells of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, which floods the marrow and blood. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma has few malignant cells, the Reed-Sternberg cells, not a flood of blasts.

Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma, about 10% of lymphomas, is characterized by few malignant Reed-Sternberg cells among numerous immune effector cells. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma makes up the other 90% and includes B-cell and T-cell types.
Plasma cells are the cell of origin of multiple myeloma, which makes a monoclonal M protein. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma is marked by a few Reed-Sternberg cells in a crowd of immune cells.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 15

set1.topic: Chronic myelogenous leukemia: management and prognosis
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: At 12 months of treatment for chronic myelogenous leukemia, the BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level is 0.05%. Which milestone category is this?
opts: At 12 months, failure needs a level above 1%, far above 0.05%. Failure means the BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level is above the worst cutoff for that month: above 10% at 6 months, above 1% at 12 months and beyond; it is not defined at 3 months.
At 12 months, warning covers 0.1-1%, and 0.05% is below that band. Warning is the middle band: above 10% at 3 months, 1-10% at 6 months, 0.1-1% at 12 months and beyond 18 months.

Correct. At 12 months, the table reads failure above 1%, warning 0.1-1% and optimal below 0.1%. A level of 0.05% is below 0.1%, so the response is optimal; treatment-free remission is not applicable at 12 months.

At 12 months the treatment-free remission column is not applicable, even for a very low level. Treatment-free remission is defined only beyond 18 months, at a BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level below 0.01%; at earlier months the column is not applicable.

set1.topic: Myelodysplastic syndrome
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: Which cytopenia is most frequent in myelodysplastic syndrome?
opts: Correct. Myelodysplastic syndrome presents most frequently with anemia, causing fatigue, weakness and pale skin; neutropenia and occasional thrombocytopenia also occur. Low-risk disease is commonly defined by anemia.
Neutropenia occurs and explains infections, but anemia is the most frequent finding. Tell: myelodysplasia usually announces itself with low red cells.
Thrombocytopenia is described as occasional in myelodysplastic syndrome, causing bleeding. Tell: anemia is the most frequent cytopenia.

A raised lymphocyte count is not a cytopenia at all; atypical lymphocytosis is a feature of infections that mimic acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: myelodysplasia lowers counts, most often red cells.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slides 45, 46, 47

set1.topic: Acute myeloid leukemia: presentation and diagnosis
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: Which test differentiates acute myeloid leukemia from acute lymphoblastic leukemia by cell markers?
opts: Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy; flow cytometry identifies the markers of the leukemia and differentiates acute myeloid from acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
Lumbar puncture is part of the acute leukemia work-up to look for central nervous system spread, not to read cell markers. Tell: it stages; flow cytometry assigns lineage.
Coagulation tests belong to the supporting blood work and matter for bleeding, especially in acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: lineage is read from markers on flow cytometry.
A chest X-ray may show a mediastinal mass in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia but cannot assign lineage. Tell: cell markers come from flow cytometry.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 36

set1.topic: Myelodysplastic syndrome
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: What does the bone marrow typically look like in myelodysplastic syndrome?
opts: Correct. In myelodysplastic syndrome the marrow is typically hypercellular, but the cells are not functional, which is why patients have cytopenias despite a full marrow.
A fibrotic marrow is the endpoint of myelofibrosis, from cytokine-driven proliferation of the myeloid lines. Tell: myelodysplastic marrow is full of cells that do not work.
A marrow with at least 20% myeloid blasts is acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: myelodysplasia stays below 20% blasts.
A marrow of malignant plasma cells is multiple myeloma, with its M protein. Tell: myelodysplasia is a myeloid disorder with dysplastic cells.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 46

set1.q: What is the median age at diagnosis of chronic myelogenous leukemia?
opts: Under 15 is where acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common malignancy. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia is a middle-aged adult disease.
Correct. The median age of chronic myelogenous leukemia is 45-55 years; it may occur in either sex but is slightly more common in men.
Over 60 is the age group for acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia has a younger median, 45-55.
A median of 70 is myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia is diagnosed at a median of 45-55.

set1.topic: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: who and why
set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for disorders of hematological malignancies in the lecture topic list for the following populations. Infant a. child b. adolescent c. adult d. elderly
set1.q: In children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, which genetic finding is common and favorable?
opts: The Philadelphia chromosome, the chromosome 9 and 22 translocation, is the most common mutation in adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia, not the favorable childhood finding. Tell: extra chromosome copies are the pediatric pattern.

The chromosome 15 and 17 translocation fuses two genes and causes acute promyelocytic leukemia, a myeloid cancer. Tell: the favorable childhood finding in acute lymphoblastic leukemia is hyperdiploidy.
A Janus kinase 2 mutation commonly causes polycythemia vera, a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Tell: a pediatric lymphoid leukemia with a good outlook points to excess chromosome copies.
Correct. Particularly in children, acute lymphoblastic leukemia often results from excess copies of a chromosome, called hyperdiploidy, which carries a favorable prognosis.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 20

set1.topic: Performance status, work-up and transplant terms
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: Which test is required in almost every hematologic malignancy to secure the correct diagnosis?
opts: A complete blood count can detect incidental cytopenias that start the work-up, but it cannot name the malignancy. Tell: abnormal counts raise the question; marrow biopsy or flow cytometry answers it.
A chemistry panel may show an elevated protein level that first hints at myeloma, but it does not confirm a diagnosis. Tell: it is a clue on routine labs, not the confirming test.

Lumbar puncture is part of the acute leukemia work-up to look for central nervous system involvement, not the diagnostic test for every blood cancer. Tell: it stages spread; marrow biopsy or flow cytometry makes the diagnosis.

Correct. Almost all hematologic malignancies require a bone marrow biopsy and/or flow cytometry as part of the work-up to ensure the correct diagnosis. Blood counts and chemistry panels may raise the suspicion but do not settle it.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slides 11, 25

set1.q: Which chemical exposure is named as a risk factor for hematologic malignancies?
opts: Aspirin is used to reduce clotting risk in essential thrombocythemia; it is not listed as a risk factor. Tell: the environmental exposures named are radiation and chemicals like benzene.

Correct. Environmental risk factors include radiation and specific chemical exposures such as benzene, alongside genetic factors, autoimmune disorders and older age. Benzene is listed again for both acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukemia.

Arsenic trioxide appears as a treatment, used with all-trans retinoic acid for acute promyelocytic leukemia, not as a named risk factor. Tell: the chemical risk factor is benzene; arsenic is on the therapy side.

Hydroxyurea is a treatment for polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia, not a listed cause. Tell: the drugs named as risks are certain chemotherapies such as alkylators; the chemical is benzene.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: What is the goal of treatment in lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome?
opts: Major molecular response is the treatment target in chronic myelogenous leukemia on tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Tell: the myelodysplasia goal is quality of life.

Correct. Lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome has a median survival above 5 years and very low risk of acute myeloid leukemia, but patients often have complications from anemia, bleeding or infections, so the goal of treatment is to improve quality of life.
Allogeneic transplant is the only curative option but is high risk with a limited role, and lower-risk disease rarely justifies it. Tell: the low-risk goal is comfort and function.
Cytarabine plus an anthracycline (7+3) is intensive chemotherapy for fit patients with acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: low-risk myelodysplasia is managed for quality of life.

set1.q: What determines whether a hematologic malignancy is lymphoid or myeloid?
opts: A high or low white count is seen in both lymphoid and myeloid leukemias, so it cannot assign the lineage. Tell: flow cytometry and marrow testing identify the cell type; the count only shows how many cells there are.

Age shifts the likelihood of a given cancer, but it does not define lineage: acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukemia both occur in adults. Tell: lineage is a property of the cancer cell, not of the patient.

Correct. Hematologic malignancies are classified into leukemias, lymphomas and plasma cell disorders, and the underlying cell of origin determines whether the type is lymphoid or myeloid. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia starts in lymphoid progenitors; acute myeloid leukemia in myeloid progenitors.

Symptoms such as fatigue, bleeding, swollen nodes or bone pain are non-specific and overlap across the families. Tell: the lineage label follows the cell the cancer started from, not how the patient feels.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 7

set1.q: For which patients is prognosis of a hematologic malignancy said to depend most on fitness?
opts: Correct. Prognosis of hematologic malignancies is often dictated by patient fitness, particularly for older patients. That is why fitness splits acute myeloid leukemia treatment into intensive chemotherapy for fit patients and low-intensity therapy for unfit ones.

Children under 15 with acute lymphoblastic leukemia have a favorable outlook with intensive regimens; fitness is singled out for older patients instead. Tell: the fitness warning is aimed at the elderly.

Neonates are noted only as the exception to the rarity of acute myeloid leukemia in children, not as the group whose outlook hinges on fitness. Tell: the performance score is emphasized for older adults.
Adolescents fall under the pediatric-like treatment of younger patients, whose outcomes are better; fitness is emphasized for the older group. Tell: the fitness point is tied to older age.

set1.topic: Acute promyelocytic leukemia
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: Which treatment is unique to acute promyelocytic leukemia?
opts: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors treat chronic myelogenous leukemia and Philadelphia-positive lymphoblastic leukemia, the chromosome 9 and 22 diseases. Tell: chromosome 15 and 17 disease gets arsenic and retinoic acid.

Correct. Acute promyelocytic leukemia has a unique treatment approach: arsenic trioxide and all-trans retinoic acid, rather than the chemotherapy used for other acute myeloid leukemia. Patients who survive the presentation have a cure rate above 90%.

Cytarabine plus an anthracycline (7+3) is intensive chemotherapy for fit patients with other acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: the promyelocytic subtype gets arsenic trioxide and all-trans retinoic acid instead.
Hypomethylating agents, with or without venetoclax, are low-intensity therapy for unfit patients with acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: the promyelocytic subtype has its own regimen.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 43

set1.topic: Hematopoiesis and the malignancy families
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: Multiple myeloma arises from which cell?
opts: Lymphoblasts are the very immature lymphoid cells of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: myeloma comes from the most mature end of the B-cell line, the terminally differentiated plasma cell.

Correct. Multiple myeloma arises from terminally differentiated B cells called plasma cells. Because plasma cells make our antibodies, myeloma produces an excess of a single monoclonal antibody, the M protein.

T cells are lymphoid cells that can give rise to T-cell lymphomas and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, not myeloma. Tell: myeloma is a plasma cell disorder, and plasma cells come from B cells, not T cells.

Myeloid progenitors give rise to acute myeloid leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and the myeloproliferative neoplasms. Tell: the name sounds myeloid, but myeloma is a lymphoid-line cancer of antibody-making plasma cells.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 16

set1.q: Which approach is used for fit patients with acute myeloid leukemia?
opts: Hypomethylating agents, with or without venetoclax, are low-intensity therapy for unfit patients. Tell: fitness decides it, and a fit patient gets intensive chemotherapy.
Arsenic trioxide with all-trans retinoic acid is the unique treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: it is reserved for the promyelocytic subtype, not acute myeloid leukemia in general.

Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark of chronic-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia and are used for Philadelphia-positive lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: fit acute myeloid leukemia gets cytarabine plus an anthracycline.

Correct. Fit patients receive intensive chemotherapy, often cytarabine plus an anthracycline (7+3). Allogeneic stem cell transplant typically follows for most intermediate- and high-risk patients who achieve remission.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: How is chronic myelogenous leukemia often discovered?
opts: Itching with warm water is the classic symptom of polycythemia vera. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia is often silent and found on a blood count.
Emergent bleeding from disseminated intravascular coagulation is the presentation of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia is often found incidentally.
A mediastinal mass is seen in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia is often an incidental high white count.

Correct. About 50% of chronic myelogenous leukemia cases are asymptomatic at diagnosis, which occurs because of leukocytosis on a complete blood count. Others present with anemia, abdominal discomfort from splenomegaly or B-symptoms.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 59

set1.topic: Chronic myelogenous leukemia: presentation, diagnosis and phases
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: In chronic myelogenous leukemia, about 14% blasts with significant splenomegaly fits which phase?
opts: Correct. The accelerated phase often has 10-19% blasts, may show dysplastic granulocytes and fibrosis, and frequently presents with significant splenomegaly; 14% blasts sits inside that band. It is about 4-5% of presentations.
The chronic (stable) phase has no or few blasts, below 5%, and makes up 85-90% of presentations. Tell: 14% blasts is far above the chronic-phase level.
Blast phase, or blast crisis, behaves as an acute leukemia, usually like acute myeloid leukemia, which is defined by 20% or more blasts. Tell: 14% is below the acute leukemia line.

Myelodysplastic syndrome also has blasts below 20%, but it presents as cytopenias, not with the marked leukocytosis and fusion gene of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: the stem names a chronic myelogenous leukemia phase question.

set1.q: Which pair of instructions is given for both polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia?
opts: Admission for work-up and treatment is the start for acute leukemia. Tell: polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia are referred to hematology with smoking cessation.
Correct. Patients with polycythemia vera and with essential thrombocythemia should be referred to a hematologist and advised to cease smoking, since both carry clotting risk.

Hydroxyurea is shared, but phlebotomy is the polycythemia vera treatment for red cell excess; essential thrombocythemia uses aspirin or hydroxyurea. Tell: the shared advice is referral and smoking cessation.
Palliative Janus kinase inhibitors are the treatment of myelofibrosis, the most aggressive myeloproliferative neoplasm. Tell: the two milder neoplasms share referral and smoking cessation.

set1.q: After stopping tyrosine kinase inhibitors in sustained major molecular response, about how often does chronic myelogenous leukemia recur?
opts: About 5% is the rate of leukemic transformation in polycythemia vera. Tell: stopping therapy in chronic myelogenous leukemia leads to recurrence in about half.
Twenty percent understates it; recurrence follows in about half of patients. Tell: discontinuation is possible but recurrence is common, about 50%.
Correct. Patients who achieve a sustained major molecular response may safely discontinue treatment, but recurrences occur in about 50% of cases; most who recur are able to recapture deep responses.
More than 80% is the five-year leukemia risk in very high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia recurs in about 50% after stopping.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: Why do patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia have bone or joint pain?
opts: Clotting from high platelets is the risk in essential thrombocythemia, with headaches, paresthesias or vision changes. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia lowers platelets; its bone pain is marrow overgrowth.

Correct. Bone or joint pain in acute lymphoblastic leukemia is due to very excessive marrow production of leukemia cells. It sits alongside anemia, bleeding, infections, B-symptoms and, in more than half, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.
Marrow fibrosis is the endpoint of myelofibrosis, which presents with splenomegaly symptoms. Tell: the pain in lymphoblastic leukemia comes from a marrow packed with blasts.
Increased blood viscosity from red cell overproduction is polycythemia vera, which causes headaches and blurry vision. Tell: bone pain in acute leukemia comes from marrow expansion, not viscosity.

set1.q: How does acute lymphoblastic leukemia differ from an aggressive lymphoma in where it is found?
opts: Severe splenomegaly with a fibrotic marrow is myelofibrosis, a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a diffuse marrow and blood disease.
Bone pain with a monoclonal M protein is multiple myeloma, a plasma cell disorder. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is immature lymphoid blasts spread through the marrow and blood.

Correct. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia often shows diffuse marrow and peripheral blood involvement, in contrast to aggressive lymphomas, which involve nodal or extranodal sites with minimal bone marrow involvement.
Nodal or extranodal disease with minimal marrow involvement describes aggressive lymphomas, the reverse of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: the leukemia fills the marrow and blood.

set1.q: On morphology, Auer rods (fused lysosomes) confirm which lineage?
opts: Correct. Morphology showing Auer rods, which are fused lysosomes, confirms a myeloid origin. Flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy confirm the diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia and separate it from acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
B-cell lineage is shown by flow cytometry markers, as in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia; Auer rods are not a lymphoid finding. Tell: Auer rods mean myeloid.
T-cell lineage is identified by flow cytometry in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, which may involve the thymus. Tell: Auer rods confirm a myeloid leukemia, not a T-cell one.
Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells, the origin of multiple myeloma, which makes an M protein. Tell: Auer rods belong to myeloid blasts.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set2.q: If a patient survives the initial presentation of acute promyelocytic leukemia, what is the cure rate?
opts: About 10% is the overall survival of adverse-risk or secondary acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: surviving promyelocytic leukemia patients do far better.
About 25-30% is the five-year survival of acute myeloid leukemia overall. Tell: the promyelocytic subtype, once past its early bleeding risk, is cured over 90% of the time.
Half understates the outlook; the cure rate after surviving presentation is above 90%. Tell: the danger is early, and the long-term outlook is excellent.

Correct. Acute promyelocytic leukemia has high early mortality from disseminated intravascular coagulation and bleeding, but if the patient survives the initial presentation, the prognosis is excellent, with a cure rate above 90%.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set2.q: Where does normal hematopoiesis begin?
opts: The spleen is a lymphoid tissue in which some lymphomas arise, and it enlarges in several myeloid cancers, but blood cell production does not begin there. Tell: the stem cell that starts hematopoiesis lives in the bone marrow.

The thymus is a lymphoid tissue where some lymphomas and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia can be found, not where hematopoiesis begins. Tell: the hematopoietic stem cell sits in the marrow, upstream of every lymphoid and myeloid line.

Correct. Normal hematopoiesis begins in the bone marrow with hematopoietic stem cells, which differentiate into myeloid and lymphoid progenitors and then into the terminally differentiated cell lines. That is why almost every blood cancer work-up includes a bone marrow biopsy.

Lymph nodes are lymphoid tissue where lymphomas often arise, not the starting point of blood cell production. Tell: hematopoiesis starts with stem cells in the marrow; lymph nodes are where lymphoma cells collect.

set2.q: Besides confirming the diagnosis, what is the BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) polymerase chain reaction assay used for?
opts: Lymph node staging belongs to lymphoma, which arises from lymphoid tissue. Tell: the fusion gene level tracks how well treatment is working.
Fitness is graded with the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance score, from the patient's daily activity. Tell: the fusion gene assay measures the disease, not the patient.
Fibrosis is seen on bone marrow biopsy, in the accelerated phase or in myelofibrosis. Tell: the polymerase chain reaction level is the response monitor.

Correct. The polymerase chain reaction assay for BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) confirms the diagnosis and is also important for monitoring response to treatment; its level at 3, 6, 12 and beyond 18 months defines the response milestones.

set2.q: Which age groups carry the highest risk of acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
opts: A median age of 45 to 55 years describes chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is bimodal, peaking in young children and again after 50.

Correct. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia has a bimodal distribution: risk is highest in children under 5 and adults over 50. It is the most common malignancy under age 15, and in adults incidence peaks around 50.
Adults over 60 are the group at risk for acute myeloid leukemia, which is unusual in children outside neonates. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia has two peaks, one of them in young children.
A median age of 70 belongs to myelodysplastic syndrome, which is often idiopathic in older people. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is bimodal, with a pediatric peak.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set2.q: How is Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated?
opts: Correct. Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia, carrying the chromosome 9 and 22 translocation, is treated with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor plus chemotherapy. Allogeneic transplant is added where feasible for adverse-risk or relapsed disease.

Arsenic trioxide with all-trans retinoic acid is the unique treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia, the chromosome 15 and 17 disease. Tell: the 9 and 22 translocation calls for a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
Phlebotomy and hydroxyurea treat polycythemia vera, which overproduces red cells. Tell: a Philadelphia-positive acute leukemia needs a tyrosine kinase inhibitor with chemotherapy.

Hypomethylating agents are low-intensity therapy for unfit patients with acute myeloid leukemia and for higher-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: the Philadelphia chromosome points to a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

set2.topic: Myelodysplastic syndrome
set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for disorders of hematological malignancies in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
set2.q: What is the median age at diagnosis of myelodysplastic syndrome?
opts: Under 15 is where acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common malignancy. Tell: myelodysplasia is a disease of older adults.
Around 50 is the adult peak of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and 45 to 55 the median of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: myelodysplasia is older, with a median of 70.
Over 60 is where acute myeloid leukemia is mostly seen. Tell: the median age for myelodysplastic syndrome is higher, 70.
Correct. Myelodysplastic syndrome is often idiopathic and occurs in an older population, with a median age of 70 years. It is more common in men and sometimes follows prior chemotherapy or radiation.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set2.q: Polycythemia vera is overproduction of which cells?
opts: Correct. Myeloproliferative neoplasms are rare myeloid malignancies with atypical proliferation of mature cell lines; polycythemia vera is over-production of red blood cells, which increases blood viscosity.
Over-production of platelets is essential thrombocythemia, which risks clotting and, paradoxically, bleeding. Tell: polycythemia means too many red cells.
Increased granulocytes, more mature than blasts, are the picture of chronic myelogenous leukemia with its Philadelphia chromosome. Tell: polycythemia vera raises the red cells.
Over-production of the mature myeloid lines, ending in marrow fibrosis, is myelofibrosis. Tell: polycythemia vera is a red cell disorder that thickens the blood.

set2.q: Which group of symptoms makes up the B-symptoms of a hematologic malignancy?
opts: Bone pain, anemia and renal dysfunction, with hypercalcemia, are the features of multiple myeloma. Tell: the myeloma set is organ damage; B-symptoms are fever, sweats and weight loss.

Correct. B-symptoms are weight loss, fever and night sweats, with loss of appetite listed too. They appear in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia and chronic myelogenous leukemia, and lymphomas often present with night sweats, weight loss and fevers.

Fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath and pale skin are the symptoms of anemia from marrow failure. Tell: these trace to low red cells; B-symptoms are systemic weight loss, fever and sweats.
Bruising, often petechiae or purpura, and bleeding are the symptoms of thrombocytopenia. Tell: they trace to low platelets, not to the systemic B-symptoms.

set2.q: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is defined by lymphoid blasts at or above what percentage of the bone marrow?
opts: Below 5% blasts describes the chronic phase of chronic myelogenous leukemia, with no or few blasts. Tell: an acute leukemia needs at least 20% blasts in the marrow.
Ten percent is the lower threshold some genetic mutations allow in acute myeloid leukemia under newer guidelines, not the definition here. Tell: lymphoblastic leukemia is defined at 20% or more.

Correct. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is defined by blast cells of lymphoid origin at or above 20% in the bone marrow, often with diffuse marrow and peripheral blood involvement. Cytogenetics and mutation analysis then refine the prognosis.
Thirty percent overstates the threshold; the definition is lymphoid blasts at or above 20%. Tell: 20% is the line used for both acute leukemias.

set2.q: Hematologic malignancies result from mutation in and proliferation of what?
opts: The initial oncogenic mutation occurs in a single somatic cell, not in every cell from birth, even though family history and genetic syndromes raise risk. Tell: genetics can raise risk, but the cancer itself is one acquired clone.

Reactive cells, as in the atypical lymphocytosis of mononucleosis or pertussis, are not clonal, and flow cytometry separates them from leukemia on that basis. Tell: reactive means a response to infection; malignant means one clone.

Correct. Hematologic malignancies are cancers of blood-forming tissues or the lymphatic system arising from mutation in and proliferation of a hematologic clone, so they are monoclonal. The first oncogenic mutation occurs in a single somatic cell, which then gains a growth advantage.
A mix of unrelated clones would be polyclonal, the opposite of the definition. Tell: the disease grows from one mutated somatic cell, which is why flow cytometry looks for clonality.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set2.q: About what is the overall five-year survival of acute myeloid leukemia?
opts: Five percent is the five-year survival of patients over 70, the lowest group. Tell: the overall figure is about 25-30%.

Correct. Treatment brings initial remission in many patients, but acute myeloid leukemia frequently relapses and treatment-related mortality is high: overall survival is only 48% at one year and about 25-30% at five years.
Forty-eight percent is the overall survival at one year, not at five years. Tell: by five years it falls to about 25-30%.
A cure rate above 90% belongs to acute promyelocytic leukemia in patients who survive the initial presentation. Tell: acute myeloid leukemia overall is about 25-30% at five years.
set2.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 41

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set2.q: What sorts acute myeloid leukemia into favorable, intermediate and poor risk?
opts: Correct. Acute myeloid leukemia shows tremendous variety in cytogenetic abnormalities and mutations, and risk is broken down into favorable, intermediate and poor on that basis. Cytogenetic and mutation analysis is important for prognosis.
The white count is often elevated but may be low, and counts above 100,000 need leukapheresis; it does not set the risk group. Tell: the risk categories come from the genetics.
The blast percentage, 20% or more, makes the diagnosis rather than the risk group. Tell: once diagnosed, cytogenetics and mutations sort the risk.

The performance grade measures fitness and steers intensive versus low-intensity therapy, but it is not the basis of the genetic risk groups. Tell: favorable, intermediate and poor risk are read from cytogenetics and mutations.

set2.q: How is myelofibrosis often treated?
opts: Arsenic trioxide with all-trans retinoic acid is the unique treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: myelofibrosis treatment is palliative Janus kinase inhibition.
Correct. Myelofibrosis is often treated with targeted inhibitors, Janus kinase inhibitors, which are palliative. Patients should be referred to a hematologist upon diagnosis.
Phlebotomy removes the red cell excess of polycythemia vera. Tell: myelofibrosis gets palliative Janus kinase inhibitors.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark therapy of chronic-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: myelofibrosis is a Janus kinase pathway disease treated with Janus kinase inhibitors.

set2.q: For an older patient with acute myeloid leukemia who is unfit for intensive chemotherapy, which treatment is used?
opts: Arsenic trioxide with all-trans retinoic acid treats acute promyelocytic leukemia specifically. Tell: the unfit acute myeloid leukemia patient gets a hypomethylating agent.
Phlebotomy and hydroxyurea treat polycythemia vera, which overproduces red cells. Tell: they do not treat acute leukemia; low-intensity therapy does.
Correct. Unfit patients receive low-intensity therapy, frequently a hypomethylating agent with or without venetoclax. Fitness matters most in older patients, and survival is lowest over age 70.
Cytarabine plus an anthracycline (7+3) is intensive chemotherapy for fit patients. Tell: an unfit patient gets low-intensity therapy instead.

set2.topic: Chronic myelogenous leukemia: who and why
set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set2.q: Before tyrosine kinase inhibitors, chronic myelogenous leukemia historically progressed to acute leukemia in about how many years?
opts: One to two years understates the historical course of about 4-6 years. Tell: under 2 years is closer to high-risk myelofibrosis survival.

Correct. Chronic myelogenous leukemia historically progressed from a chronic condition to acute leukemia in about 4-6 years and was considered fatal; with tyrosine kinase inhibitors it is now largely a chronic disorder with long-term survival.
Ten to fifteen years is how long low-risk myelofibrosis patients can live. Tell: untreated chronic myelogenous leukemia historically turned acute in about 4-6 years.
Fourteen years is the estimated survival of polycythemia vera. Tell: the historical chronic myelogenous leukemia figure is about 4-6 years to acute leukemia.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set2.q: From what does myelodysplastic syndrome often evolve?
opts: Correct. Myelodysplastic syndrome often evolves from progression of milder abnormal stem cell clones, called clonal hematopoiesis, until the dysplasia characteristic of the syndrome develops.

The direction is reversed: myelodysplastic syndrome can progress to acute myeloid leukemia, and very high-risk disease has over 80% risk within 5 years. Tell: myelodysplasia comes before leukemia, not after.
Viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus are listed risks for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, not the origin of myelodysplasia. Tell: myelodysplasia grows out of milder abnormal clones.
A reactive leukocytosis is a response to infection and is not clonal. Tell: myelodysplasia starts from clonal hematopoiesis, an abnormal clone.

set2.q: What distinguishes an acute leukemia from a chronic leukemia?
opts: Correct. Acute leukemias arise from more immature, progenitor white blood cells and cause rapid proliferation of that clone. Chronic leukemias involve proliferation of mature malignant white blood cells.
Proliferation of mature malignant white cells is the definition of a chronic leukemia. Tell: acute means immature progenitors growing fast; chronic means mature cells.
Myeloid versus lymphoid is decided by the cell of origin, and both acute and chronic leukemias come in myeloid forms. Tell: lineage and tempo are separate labels; acute refers to immature cells.
Lymph node involvement is the hallmark of lymphoma, which arises from lymphoid tissue. Tell: a leukemia is a marrow disease; acute versus chronic depends on how immature the cells are.

set2.q: Which test separates acute lymphoblastic leukemia from the atypical lymphocytosis of mononucleosis or pertussis?
opts: Correct. Some infections, including mononucleosis and pertussis, cause atypical lymphocytosis, and flow cytometry differentiates these from acute lymphoblastic leukemia based on its clonal nature. It also shows whether the leukemia is B-cell or T-cell.
Lumbar puncture checks for central nervous system involvement, an adverse risk factor, after the diagnosis is made. Tell: it stages the leukemia; it does not show whether lymphocytes are clonal.
A chest X-ray may show a mediastinal mass in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, but it cannot tell reactive from malignant lymphocytes. Tell: clonality is read by flow cytometry.
Coagulation tests are part of the wider acute leukemia work-up and matter for bleeding complications. Tell: separating a clone from a reactive infection needs flow cytometry.

set2.q: How is a patient with newly diagnosed acute leukemia usually first managed?
opts: Acute leukemia requires referral to and management by a hematologist/oncologist, not primary-care follow-up. Tell: the specialist and the hospital admission come first.
Started on oral therapy at home
Oral tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark of chronic-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia, managed as a chronic disorder. Tell: acute leukemia starts with admission for work-up and treatment.

Correct. Most patients with acute leukemia are initially admitted for work-up and initiation of treatment, under a hematologist/oncologist, ideally a specialist in the disease. Frequent follow-up, lifelong surveillance and clinical trials follow.
Watching with repeat counts is not the approach to an acute leukemia, which proliferates rapidly from immature cells. Tell: acute leukemia means admission and prompt treatment.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set2.q: What share of chronic myelogenous leukemia presentations are in chronic phase?
opts: About 1-2% is the share of blast phase, the acute-leukemia-like stage. Tell: most patients present in the stable chronic phase.
About 4-5% is the share of the accelerated phase. Tell: the chronic phase is the large majority, 85-90%.
About 50% is the share of cases asymptomatic at diagnosis, not the chronic-phase share. Tell: chronic phase is 85-90% of presentations.
Correct. The chronic (stable) phase accounts for 85-90% of all presentations and carries an excellent prognosis. The accelerated phase is about 4-5% and blast phase about 1-2%.

set2.topic: Chronic myelogenous leukemia: who and why
set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set2.q: Chronic myelogenous leukemia produces increased numbers of which cells?
opts: Plasma cells are the origin of multiple myeloma, which makes an M protein. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia is a granulocyte disorder.

Correct. Chronic myelogenous leukemia originates from hematopoietic stem cells but produces increased numbers of granulocytes, which are more mature than blasts. The marrow shows marked granulocytic proliferation and myelocytes in chronic phase.
Lymphoblasts, very immature lymphoid cells, are the cells of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: chronic means more mature cells, and myelogenous means the granulocyte line.
Red cell overproduction is polycythemia vera; in chronic myelogenous leukemia red cell morphology is normal and the hematocrit is not elevated. Tell: the excess here is granulocytes.

set2.q: Which treatment is used to reduce clotting risk in essential thrombocythemia?
opts: Phlebotomy lowers the red cell excess of polycythemia vera. Tell: essential thrombocythemia is a platelet problem treated with aspirin or hydroxyurea.
Adding platelets would raise an already high count. Tell: the goal in essential thrombocythemia is to reduce clotting risk, with aspirin or hydroxyurea.
Arsenic trioxide with all-trans retinoic acid treats acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: essential thrombocythemia uses aspirin or hydroxyurea.
Correct. Essential thrombocythemia is treated with aspirin, hydroxyurea or other agents to reduce clotting risk, and patients are referred to a hematologist and advised to cease smoking.

set2.q: How is blast-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia treated?
opts: Correct. Blast phase, or blast crisis, behaves as an acute leukemia, usually like acute myeloid leukemia, often with unique chromosomal and mutational changes; it requires acute myeloid leukemia-like regimens and responds poorly to tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
A tyrosine kinase inhibitor by itself
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark of chronic-phase therapy, but blast phase responds poorly to them. Tell: blast crisis is treated like an acute leukemia.
Watching would ignore a stage that behaves as an acute leukemia with median survival under 12 months. Tell: blast phase needs acute myeloid leukemia-like treatment.
Stopping tyrosine kinase inhibitors is considered only after a sustained major molecular response in chronic-phase disease. Tell: blast phase needs intensive acute leukemia-like treatment.

set2.q: How often does polycythemia vera transform to leukemia?
opts: Correct. Polycythemia vera has an excellent prognosis, with an estimated survival of 14 years, and rarely results in leukemic transformation, in about 5% of cases.
A quarter overstates it; transformation is rare, about 5%. Tell: polycythemia vera is the low-risk member of the myeloproliferative neoplasms.
About 50% is the recurrence rate after stopping tyrosine kinase inhibitors in chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: polycythemia vera transforms in about 5%.
More than 80% within 5 years is the leukemia risk of very high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: polycythemia vera rarely transforms.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set2.q: Which acute myeloid leukemia subtypes may show gum hyperplasia or other extramedullary disease?
opts: Undifferentiated acute myeloid leukemia and the minimal-maturation subtype are the least mature forms and are not tied to gum disease. Tell: gum hyperplasia means myelomonocytic or monocytic.
Correct. The myelomonocytic and monocytic subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia tend to have more extramedullary involvement, and they may involve the gums (hyperplasia).
Acute promyelocytic leukemia is known for emergent disseminated intravascular coagulation and bleeding, not gum involvement. Tell: gums point to the monocytic subtypes.
Acute erythroid and acute megakaryocytic leukemias are very rare subtypes, not the ones linked to gum involvement. Tell: extramedullary disease is a monocytic-line feature.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set2.q: In a hematologic malignancy, bleeding is usually due to which count abnormality?
opts: Anemia explains fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath and pale skin, not bleeding. Tell: tiredness points to red cells; bleeding points to platelets.
Too few working white cells explains infections, not bleeding. Tell: infections follow ineffective or low white cells, while bruising and bleeding follow low platelets.

A high white count reflects proliferation of the leukemic clone itself; it does not cause bleeding by the stated mechanism. Tell: bleeding is listed under thrombocytopenia, with petechiae and purpura.

Correct. Hematologic malignancies often present with non-specific symptoms: fatigue from anemia, bleeding from thrombocytopenia, swollen nodes in lymphoma and bone pain in myeloma. Low platelets explain the bruising and bleeding.

set2.q: What does an allogeneic stem cell transplant use?
opts: Red cell transfusions are supportive care, for example in lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome with anemia; they do not replace the marrow. Tell: a transplant gives stem cells that rebuild the marrow, not mature blood cells.
Growth factors such as erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and myeloid growth factors push the existing marrow; they are not a transplant. Tell: a transplant replaces the stem cells themselves.

Correct. An allogeneic stem cell transplant uses a healthy donor's stem cells. It is the transplant used for adverse-risk or relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia and is the only curative therapy for myelodysplastic syndrome.
Using the person's own stem cells is an autologous transplant, also called stem cell rescue, often given to rescue the marrow after high-dose chemotherapy. Tell: auto means self; allo means a donor.

set2.q: Under newer guidelines, certain genetic mutations allow acute myeloid leukemia to be diagnosed with myeloid blasts at or above what percentage?
opts: One percent is a BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) milestone level in chronic myelogenous leukemia monitoring, not a blast threshold. Tell: the mutation-based exception is 10%.
Below 5% blasts is the chronic phase of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: the genetic exception for acute myeloid leukemia lowers the line to 10%, not 5%.

Correct. Historically, acute myeloid leukemia required myeloid blasts at or above 20%, but newer guidelines note that certain genetic mutations may allow the diagnosis with only 10% or higher. That is why cytogenetic and mutation analysis matters at diagnosis.
Twenty percent is the historical definition, not the lower threshold allowed for certain mutations. Tell: the exception is 10% or higher.

set2.q: Very high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome carries what risk of developing acute myeloid leukemia within 5 years?
opts: About 5% is the leukemic transformation rate of polycythemia vera. Tell: very high-risk myelodysplasia transforms far more often, over 80%.
A quarter understates the risk; very high-risk disease overlaps substantially with acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: the figure is over 80%.
Half understates it. About 50% is instead the recurrence rate after stopping tyrosine kinase inhibitors in chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: very high-risk myelodysplasia exceeds 80%.

Correct. Very high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome has a median overall survival of 9 months and more than 80% risk of developing acute myeloid leukemia within 5 years. Lower-risk disease has a median survival above 5 years and very low leukemia risk.

set2.q: What is the classic symptom of polycythemia vera?
opts: Early satiety, bloating and abdominal pain from splenomegaly are the presentation of myelofibrosis. Tell: itching after a warm bath is the polycythemia vera clue.
Gum involvement (hyperplasia) is seen in the myelomonocytic and monocytic subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: the polycythemia vera clue is itch with warm water.
Bone or joint pain from excessive marrow production of leukemia cells is a feature of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: polycythemia vera classically itches after warm baths or showers.
Correct. Polycythemia vera usually presents non-specifically with fatigue, headaches and blurry vision, but the classic symptom is pruritus with warm baths or showers.
